name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Linkage group formed by genes on chromosome

questiontext.text: All genes located on the same chromosome:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A linkage group consists of all the genes that are physically located on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together during cell division.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because a single chromosome is composed of a continuous linear molecule of DNA, all genes present on that particular chromosome are linked together and collectively constitute a single linkage group. The number of linkage groups in any organism corresponds to its haploid chromosome number.

Step 3: Conclusion
Thus, all genes located on the same chromosome form one linkage group.

answer.text: Form different groups depending upon their relative distance
Form interactive groups that affect the phenotype

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Condition of karyotype with gain or loss

questiontext.text: Conditions of a karyotype \(2n + 1\), \(2n - 1\) and \(2n + 2\), \(2n - 2\) are called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aneuploidy is the chromosomal aberration in which there is an abnormal chromosome number resulting from the gain or loss of one or more individual chromosomes during cell division, rather than entire sets.

Step 2: Evaluation
In an organism with a standard diploid complement (\(2n\)):
• \(2n + 1\) represents the gain of a single extra chromosome (trisomy).
• \(2n - 1\) represents the loss of a single chromosome (monosomy).
• \(2n + 2\) represents the gain of an extra pair of chromosomes (tetrasomy).
• \(2n - 2\) represents the loss of a homologous pair of chromosomes (nullisomy).
Since each of these conditions involves numerical changes in individual chromosomes rather than multiplication of the complete genome set, they are all classified under aneuploidy.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, conditions of karyotypes \(2n + 1\), \(2n - 1\), \(2n + 2\), and \(2n - 2\) are called aneuploidy.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q03 - Relationship between gene distance and recombination frequency

questiontext.text: Distance between the genes and percentage of recombination shows:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the chromosome theory of linkage and genetic mapping established by Alfred Sturtevant, the frequency of crossing over between linked genes is a function of the physical distance separating them on a chromosome.

Step 2: Evaluation
As the physical distance between two genes on a chromosome increases, the likelihood of chiasma formation and crossing over between them during meiotic prophase I increases proportionately. Consequently, greater distance produces a higher percentage of recombinant gametes, whereas closely linked genes experience fewer crossover events and yield a lower recombination frequency.

Step 3: Conclusion
Hence, the distance between genes and the percentage of recombination exhibits a direct relationship.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q04 - Mode of inheritance of sex linked disease

questiontext.text: If a genetic disease is transferred from a phenotypically normal but carrier female to only some of the male progeny, the disease is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In sex-linked (X-linked) recessive inheritance, females have two X chromosomes (\(X^A X^a\)) and can carry the mutant allele without expressing the disorder due to the presence of the normal dominant allele. Males possess only a single X chromosome (\(XY\)) and are hemizygous, so the presence of a single recessive mutant allele leads directly to disease expression.

Step 2: Evaluation
A carrier female has genotype \(X^A X^a\). When crossed with a normal male (\(X^A Y\)), each son receives a Y chromosome from the father and has a 50% chance of receiving the mutant \(X^a\) allele from the mother. Sons who inherit \(X^a\) (\(X^a Y\)) express the disease, while sons who inherit \(X^A\) (\(X^A Y\)) are completely normal. Female progeny receive a normal \(X^A\) allele from the father and thus remain phenotypically normal.

Step 3: Conclusion
This transmission pattern from a phenotypically normal carrier female specifically to a fraction of her male offspring identifies the disorder as sex-linked recessive.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q05 - Codon triplet coding for valine in sickle cell

questiontext.text: In sickle cell anaemia glutamic acid is replaced by valine. Which one of the following triplets codes for valine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting from a point mutation in the gene coding for the \(\beta\)-globin chain of haemoglobin.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the wild-type \(Hb^A\) gene, the sixth codon of the \(\beta\)-globin mRNA is GAG, which specifies glutamic acid. In the sickle-cell mutant \(Hb^S\) gene, a transversion mutation substitutes thymine for adenine in the DNA template strand (CTC to CAC), resulting in a transcription change from GAG to GUG on the mRNA strand. The triplet codon GUG specifies the amino acid valine instead of glutamic acid at the sixth position.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, the triplet codon coding for valine in sickle-cell anaemia is G U G.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q06 - Co dominance observed in blood group AB

questiontext.text: Person having genotype \(I^A I^B\) would show the blood group as AB. This is because of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Co-dominance occurs when two distinct alleles of a gene at a locus are equally and independently expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygous individual, without either allele masking the effect of the other.

Step 2: Evaluation
Human ABO blood groups are determined by the gene \(I\). The alleles \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) each produce a specific, functional glycosyltransferase enzyme that adds distinctive sugar antigens (A antigen and B antigen, respectively) to the surface of erythrocytes. In an individual with the heterozygous genotype \(I^A I^B\), both alleles express their corresponding antigens simultaneously and equally, resulting in the AB blood group phenotype.

Step 3: Conclusion
Because both alleles are co-expressed fully without dominance or blending, the AB phenotype is an example of co-dominance.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Species showing ZZ ZW sex determination mechanism

questiontext.text: Z Z / ZW type of sex determination is seen in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ZZ / ZW sex-determination mechanism represents female heterogamety. In this system, males possess two homomorphic sex chromosomes (ZZ) and produce a single type of gamete, while females possess two heteromorphic sex chromosomes (ZW) and produce two distinct types of ova.

Step 2: Evaluation
Female heterogamety of the ZZ / ZW type is widely characteristic of avian species (birds), as well as certain reptiles and lepidopteran insects. Among the given options, the peacock (Pavo cristatus) belongs to class Aves (birds), meaning the female peahen is ZW and the male peacock is ZZ. Mammals such as the platypus display male heterogamety (XY), and insects such as cockroaches operate via an XX / XO mechanism.

Step 3: Conclusion
Thus, the ZZ / ZW type of sex determination is seen in the peacock.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q08 - Parental genotypes yielding tall and dwarf offspring

questiontext.text: A cross between two tall plants resulted in offspring having few dwarf plants. What would be the genotypes of both the parents?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In pea plants, plant height is controlled by a single gene where the allele for tallness (\(T\)) is dominant over the allele for dwarfness (\(t\)). A plant expressing the recessive dwarf phenotype must have the homozygous recessive genotype \(tt\).

Step 2: Evaluation
To yield a dwarf offspring (\(tt\)), each parent must contribute one recessive allele (\(t\)). Since both parents are phenotypically tall, each parent must carry at least one dominant allele (\(T\)). Therefore, each parent must have one dominant allele \(T\) to account for its tall phenotype and one recessive allele \(t\) to transmit to the dwarf progeny. A cross between two heterozygous tall plants (\(Tt \times Tt\)) produces offspring with genotypes \(TT\), \(Tt\), and \(tt\) in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, generating both tall and dwarf phenotypes in a 3 : 1 ratio.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, the genotypes of both tall parents must be Tt and Tt.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Significance of dihybrid phenotypic ratio nine three three one

questiontext.text: In a dihybrid cross, if you get 9:3:3:1 ratio it denotes that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment asserts that during gamete formation, the segregation of alleles of one gene pair occurs entirely independently of the segregation of alleles of another gene pair.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a monohybrid cross with complete dominance, the phenotypic ratio in the \(F_2\) generation is 3 : 1. If two gene pairs assort independently, the combined phenotypic outcome is the product of their individual probabilities:
\[(3 : 1) \times (3 : 1) = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1\]
Obtaining this classic Mendelian dihybrid ratio confirms that the two genes reside on non-homologous chromosomes and that their alleles segregate independently without linkage, epistasis, or interaction.

Step 3: Conclusion
Hence, the 9:3:3:1 ratio denotes that the alleles of two genes are segregating independently.

answer.text: The alleles of two genes are interacting with each other
It is a case of multiple allelism
The alleles of two genes are segregating independently.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q10 - Factor that reduces genetic variation among siblings

questiontext.text: Which of the following will not result in variations among siblings?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetic variation among progeny is produced by mechanisms that create novel combinations of maternal and paternal alleles or generate novel nucleotide sequences. These mechanisms include independent assortment during meiosis, homologous crossing over during pachytene, and random mutations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Linkage describes the physical co-localization of genes on the same chromosome that causes them to be transmitted together as an intact parental unit during meiosis. By holding existing allele combinations together, linkage limits crossing over, decreases recombinant gamete formation, and preserves parental combinations, thereby restricting variation rather than creating it.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, linkage will not result in variations among siblings.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q11 - Independent assortment of non homologous chromosomes

questiontext.text: Mendel's Law of independent assortment holds good for genes situated on the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cytological basis of independent assortment is the random alignment and segregation of different bivalents (pairs of homologous chromosomes) during metaphase I and anaphase I of meiosis.

Step 2: Evaluation
Genes situated on different, non-homologous pairs of chromosomes assort independently because the orientation of one bivalent on the equatorial plate has no bearing on the orientation of another bivalent. In contrast, genes situated on the same chromosome are physically linked and do not assort independently unless separated by extensive recombination, while alleles of the same gene are located on homologous chromosomes.

Step 3: Conclusion
Consequently, Mendel's law of independent assortment holds strictly true for genes situated on non-homologous chromosomes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q12 - Single gene expressing multiple distinct phenotypic effects

questiontext.text: Occasionally, a single gene may express more than one effect. The phenomenon is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pleiotropy refers to the condition where a single gene product participates in multiple distinct physiological or biochemical pathways, thereby influencing more than one phenotypic characteristic.

Step 2: Evaluation
A well-known example of pleiotropy in humans is phenylketonuria, which is caused by a mutation in the gene coding for phenylalanine hydroxylase. The enzymatic defect manifests as intellectual disability, reduced hair growth, and decreased skin pigmentation. This is distinct from polygenic inheritance (where multiple genes control one trait) and multiple allelism (where more than two alleles of a gene exist across a population).

Step 3: Conclusion
Hence, the phenomenon in which a single gene controls more than one phenotypic effect is called pleiotropy.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q13 - Sex determination in insects with seventeen chromosomes

questiontext.text: In a certain taxon of insects some have 17 chromosomes and the others have 18 chromosomes. The 17 and 18 chromosome-bearing organisms are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In many insects, such as grasshoppers, sex determination is of the XX / XO type. In this system, females possess two X chromosomes (homogametic, XX), whereas males possess only a single X chromosome without a matching homologue (heterogametic, XO).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because both sexes possess the same set of autosomes (\(2A\)):
• Females have two sex chromosomes: \(2A + XX\), giving an even total chromosome number of 18 (meaning \(2A = 16\) autosomes and \(2\) sex chromosomes).
• Males possess only one sex chromosome: \(2A + XO\), giving an odd total chromosome number of 17 (meaning \(16\) autosomes and \(1\) sex chromosome).
Consequently, individuals with 17 chromosomes are males, and those with 18 chromosomes are females.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, the 17 and 18 chromosome-bearing organisms are males and females, respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q14 - Character studied through human pedigree analysis

questiontext.text: The inheritance pattern of a gene over generations among humans is studied by the pedigree analysis. Character studied in the pedigree analysis is equivalent to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pedigree analysis is a diagnostic and analytical method in human genetics used to trace the transmission of particular inherited traits over successive ancestral generations within a family lineage.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pedigree charts are designed to trace discontinuous, qualitative traits that are governed by single gene loci conforming to Mendelian principles of segregation and dominance (such as cystic fibrosis, haemophilia, or sickle-cell anaemia). In contrast, quantitative and polygenic traits show continuous phenotypic variation under the cumulative action of many genes and environmental factors, which cannot be categorized into discrete Mendelian inheritance patterns in standard pedigree charts.

Step 3: Conclusion
Thus, the character traced in pedigree analysis corresponds to a Mendelian trait.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q15 - Evidence for discrete non blending Mendelian factors

questiontext.text: It is said that Mendel proposed that the factor controlling any character is discrete and independent. His proposition was based on the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Prior to Mendel, inheritance was widely thought to occur via blending of parental humours or fluids, which would lead to an irreversible dilution of contrasting traits.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mendel disproved blending inheritance by observing that when pure-breeding parents with contrasting characters were crossed, the first filial (\(F_1\)) generation displayed only one of the two parental traits without any intermediate blending. Furthermore, when these \(F_1\) plants were self-pollinated, the hidden recessive trait reappeared unaltered in the \(F_2\) generation. This demonstrated that the underlying hereditary factors remain discrete, particulate units that maintain their integrity across generations.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, Mendel's proposition was rooted in the observation that the offspring of a cross between plants with contrasting characters display only one character without any blending.

answer.text: observations that the offspring of a cross made between the plants having two contrasting characters shows only one character without any blending.
cross pollination of \(F_1\) generation with recessive parent

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q16 - Test cross ratio for completely linked genes

questiontext.text: Two genes 'A' and 'B' are linked. In a dihybrid cross involving these two genes, the \(F_1\) heterozygote is crossed with homozygous recessive parental type (\(aa\,bb\)). What would be the ratio of offspring in the next generation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Genes \(A\) and \(B\) are linked on the same chromosome. The \(F_1\) dihybrid heterozygote has genotype \(AB / ab\) and is crossed with the homozygous recessive parent \(ab / ab\) (a dihybrid test cross).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Under complete linkage (where no crossing over occurs between the two loci), the linked genes travel together during meiosis into gametes as parental combinations.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
• The \(F_1\) heterozygote produces only two gametic types in equal frequencies: \(AB\) and \(ab\) (ratio 1 : 1).
• The homozygous recessive parent produces exclusively \(ab\) gametes.
• Union of these gametes produces two progeny classes:
\(AB / ab\) (dominant phenotype) and \(ab / ab\) (recessive phenotype) in a 1 : 1 ratio.
If the genes were unlinked, independent assortment would have yielded four phenotypic classes in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Because linkage prevents the formation of recombinant classes, the resulting offspring ratio is 1 : 1.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q17 - Number of phenotypes and genotypes in dihybrid cross

questiontext.text: In the \(F_2\) generation of a Mendelian dihybrid cross the number of phenotypes and genotypes are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A standard Mendelian dihybrid cross involving two gene pairs with complete dominance (\(AaBb \times AaBb\)) assorting independently.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a cross involving \(n\) independently assorting gene pairs with complete dominance:
• Number of distinct \(F_2\) phenotypes = \(2^n\)
• Number of distinct \(F_2\) genotypes = \(3^n\)
• Number of total zygotic combinations in the Punnett square = \(4^n\)

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
For a dihybrid cross (\(n = 2\)):
• Number of phenotypes = \(2^2 = 4\) (expressed in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1).
• Number of genotypes = \(3^2 = 9\) (expressed in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 4 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 1).
Although there are 16 total fertilization combinations, several combinations are genetically identical, condensing into 9 unique genotypes.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the \(F_2\) generation contains 4 phenotypes and 9 genotypes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q18 - Heterozygous parents of child with blood group O

questiontext.text: Mother and father of a person with 'O' blood group have 'A' and 'B' blood group, respectively. What would be the genotype of both mother and father?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The child has blood group O, which corresponds to the homozygous recessive genotype \(ii\). The mother has blood group A, and the father has blood group B.

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
In the ABO system, the alleles \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) are co-dominant to each other and completely dominant over allele \(i\). A person with blood group O must inherit an allele \(i\) from each biological parent.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
• For the child to have genotype \(ii\), both parents must be carriers of the recessive allele \(i\).
• The mother expresses blood group A, meaning she has at least one \(I^A\) allele. Since she must also provide an allele \(i\), her genotype must be \(I^A i\) (heterozygous for 'A').
• The father expresses blood group B, meaning he has at least one \(I^B\) allele. Since he must also provide an allele \(i\), his genotype must be \(I^B i\) (heterozygous for 'B').
If either parent were homozygous (\(I^A I^A\) or \(I^B I^B\)), that parent could only pass on a dominant allele, precluding the birth of a child with blood group O.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, both the mother and father are heterozygous for 'A' and 'B' blood group, respectively.

answer.text: Mother is homozygous for 'A' blood group and father is heterozygous for 'B'
Mother is heterozygous for 'A' blood group and father is homozygous for 'B'
Both mother and father are heterozygous for 'A' and 'B' blood group, respectively
Both mother and father are homozygous for 'A' and 'B' blood group, respectively
